main_content:
Welcome to the bra size guide — the single page that links every size, every fit problem, every measurement method, and every conversion chart on Breast Calculator. Whether you are looking up your own size, trying to solve a specific fit problem, or simply curious about how cup sizing works, this hub is your starting point.

Below you will find: a step-by-step how to measure bra size guide, a cup-size explainer, a list of common fit problems with their solutions, and a complete index of all 21 size-specific pages we maintain.

How to Measure Your Bra Size (Step-by-Step)

Measuring your bra size at home takes about 5 minutes with a soft measuring tape and a mirror. Follow these three steps in order:

  1. Measure the band. Wrap the tape snugly around your ribcage, directly underneath the breast fold. The number in inches (rounded to the nearest even number) is your band size.
  2. Measure the bust. Wrap the tape loosely around the fullest part of the breast, keeping it level. Round to the nearest inch.
  3. Calculate the cup. Subtract the band from the bust. Each inch of difference is one cup letter: 1" = A, 2" = B, 3" = C, 4" = D, 5" = DD, and so on.

For a deeper walkthrough with photos, see the how-to-measure article or use the bra size calculator to do the math for you.

Bra Cup Size Explained

A cup letter is the relative difference between your bust and your band, not an absolute volume. This is why two people who both wear a 36C can have different cup volumes — and why a 38B can look like a 36C on a longer torso.

Common Bra Fit Problems (and How to Fix Them)

Most bra discomfort comes from one of five issues. Click each one to read the full fix guide.

  • Band problems — riding up, digging in, or stretching out within weeks.
  • Cup problems — spillage, wrinkling, gaping, or sitting on top of the breast tissue.
  • Strap problems — slipping, digging in, or carrying too much of the weight.
  • Underwire & gore — wires poking, gore floating, or wires sitting on breast tissue.
  • Special cases — asymmetric, post-surgery, athletic, and maternity.

Sister Sizes & UK vs US

Two sizes share the same cup volume if they are one band apart and one cup letter apart. A 36C and a 34D are sister sizes. Going up a band means going down a cup letter. Use sister sizes when your usual size is out of stock, when you sit between band sizes, or when a band is too tight but the cup fits. Why 80% of Women Wear the Wrong Bra Size

Research from the University of Portsmouth, among others, has repeatedly found that 70–80% of women are wearing the wrong size — most often a band that is too big and a cup that is too small. The most common cause is not measuring: women rely on a size they were fitted for years ago, or they pick a size off the rack based on a sister or friend.

The fix is simple: re-measure every 6–12 months. Use the bra size calculator as a starting point, then try at least three sizes in your sister-size range before deciding. Read the full research summary in why 80% of women wear the wrong bra size.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most common bra size?

In the US, the most frequently purchased size is 36C, though average breast volume is closer to a 34DD. The discrepancy comes from people wearing bands that are too large.

How do I know if my cup is too small?

Tell-tale signs: spillage at the top or sides, the breast sitting on top of the cup rather than filling it, "double-boob" through a T-shirt, or the underwire sitting on breast tissue at the front.

How do I know if my band is too big?

Two checks: (1) the band should stay in place when you raise your arms above your head; (2) you should be able to fit only two fingers under the band, not the whole hand. If both fail, go down a band (and up a cup letter).

What is a sister size?

See above. A sister size has the same cup volume but a different band length.

How often should I re-measure?

Every 6–12 months, or after any significant weight change, pregnancy, or surgery.

Should I get professionally fitted?

If you can — yes. A professional fitting is the gold standard, especially after surgery, pregnancy, or major weight change. The calculator is a good starting point but not a replacement.

Methodology & Editorial Review

This guide aggregates measurement methods and fit-research from peer-reviewed studies, lingerie-fitting literature, and surveys conducted by the Breast Calculator Editorial Team. The most-cited source is the 2008 Portsmouth study on bra fit, plus the Inami, Qiao, and BREAST-V volumetric studies for cup-size conversion.
